description: Worked examples for the Cognitive Biases Decision Review contract. They show calibrated candidate lenses rather than diagnosing people or teams.

examples.input: We should migrate to technology X because several competitors are using it.

review.decision: Whether to migrate to technology X.
observedFacts: Several competitors are reported to use technology X.

inferredRisks.rationale: Competitor adoption may be used mainly as support for an option that is already preferred.
The competitor choice may become an early reference point before our own criteria are fixed.

missingEvidence: Evidence that competitor conditions are comparable to ours.
questions: Which criteria were fixed before looking at competitors?
What evidence would make us reject technology X?

techniques.why: Compare options against the same requirements.
Build the strongest evidence-based case against the preferred migration.

review.nextAction: Define the criteria and run the same evidence check on technology X and one serious alternative.
review.uncertainty: Competitor adoption alone does not show whether technology X fits this organisation.

examples.input: The project is late, but we have already spent too much to stop now.

review.decision: Whether to fund the next stage of the late project.

inferredRisks.rationale: Past investment is explicitly being used as a reason for future investment.

missingEvidence: Expected future value and probability of achieving it.
questions: Would we fund the next stage if the project arrived today with no history?
Which criteria should the next stage meet?

techniques.why: Separate unrecoverable past spending from future cost and value.
Judge the next stage against criteria fixed before the continuation decision.

review.nextAction: Recalculate the decision using future costs, future value and explicit continuation criteria.
review.uncertainty: Past investment can contain information about future capability, but unrecoverable cost is not itself future value.

examples.input: The AI says the migration should take 40 days. Help me refine that estimate.

observedFacts: An AI system produced an initial estimate of 40 days.

inferredRisks.rationale: The first number may pull later estimates even when its basis is unclear.
The generated recommendation may receive more weight than its evidence supports.

missingEvidence: Inspectable sources or comparable work supporting the estimate.
questions: What estimate would we make before seeing 40 days?
What evidence produced the AI number?

techniques.why: Create an estimate before using the generated number as evidence.
Trace important claims and numbers to inspectable evidence.

review.nextAction: Create an independent estimate, then trace the AI estimate to evidence before updating the range.
review.uncertainty: The AI estimate may be useful, but its reliability is unknown until its assumptions and evidence are checked.

examples.input: After the outage it is obvious that the team should have known this dependency would fail.

review.decision: What process lesson should be taken from the outage?

inferredRisks.rationale: Knowledge of the outcome can make the failure path feel more predictable than it was beforehand.
The bad outcome may replace a review of the information and process available at the decision point.

missingEvidence: Alternative failure modes that were plausible at the time.
questions: What was actually known before the dependency failed?
Would the original process look poor if the outage had not happened?

techniques.why: Compare the review with records created before the outcome.
Test the preferred causal story against credible alternatives.

review.nextAction: Reconstruct the timeline using only information available at each decision point before changing the process.
review.uncertainty: A preventable outage can still coexist with hindsight effects; the review should test both possibilities.

examples.input: I have seen the same claim on six sites, so it is probably well supported.

review.decision: How much confidence to place in the repeated claim.
observedFacts: The claim appears on six sites.

inferredRisks.rationale: Repeated exposure can increase familiarity without adding independent evidence.

missingEvidence: Whether the six sites rely on independent sources.
questions: How many independent sources are there?
Do the sites trace back to one original claim?

techniques.why: Separate independent evidence from repeated copies.
State what evidence would increase or reduce confidence.

review.nextAction: Trace the six mentions to their original sources and count independent evidence rather than repetitions.
review.uncertainty: Repetition does not prove the claim is false; it only fails to establish independence by itself.

examples.input: I have spent twelve years in this field, so changing direction now would waste all that time.

review.decision: Whether to stay in the current field or test a different direction.
observedFacts: Twelve years have already been invested in the current field.

inferredRisks.rationale: Past investment is being treated as a reason to continue regardless of the next step's value.

missingEvidence: Future value and cost of alternatives.
questions: Which next year would be best if the past could not be changed?
What small test can reduce uncertainty about the alternative?

techniques.why: Judge the next period by future value rather than unrecoverable time.
Gather evidence about another path before making a large commitment.

review.nextAction: Compare the next twelve months of each option and design one small test of the strongest alternative.
review.uncertainty: Past experience can create skills and switching costs, so it can still matter as current evidence.

examples.input: The employee missed the last delivery, so the annual performance rating should be low.

observedFacts: The employee missed the most recent delivery.

inferredRisks.rationale: The most recent and vivid event may receive more weight than the full review period.
The delivery outcome may stand in for a review of the underlying work and process.

missingEvidence: Performance evidence across the full period.
questions: What evidence represents the full review period?
What evidence supports a materially different rating?

techniques.why: Use the same role criteria across the full period.
Look for evidence that supports a different conclusion.

review.nextAction: Review the full period against predefined criteria before assigning the rating.
review.uncertainty: The missed delivery may be important; the review should test its weight rather than automatically discount it.

examples.input: Give me one exact launch date. We need a number for the plan.

review.decision: Choose how to represent the launch forecast.
observedFacts: The plan currently requests one exact launch date.

inferredRisks.rationale: Breaking uncertainty into parts may reveal uncertainty hidden by one headline estimate.
A recent delivery may dominate the estimate if a broader reference class is not used.

questions: What range is supported by comparable launches?
Which dependencies push the date toward either end?

techniques.why: Ground the forecast in completed comparable cases.
Make later changes traceable to new evidence.

review.nextAction: Publish a forecast range with assumptions and an update trigger before choosing a planning date inside it.
review.uncertainty: Planning may still require one date, but that date should not erase the underlying forecast uncertainty.
